From a <1>straw hut</1> to an international institution

In 1966, Sri Swamiji moved to the present site of the Mysuru Ashram on Ooty Road, which in the early days was only a straw hut in a field. The land was barren and infested with cobras and scorpions; Sri Swamiji slept under the trees on the bare ground with these creatures crawling all around Him. He was never harmed.

It was there, at Mysuru, that Sri Swamiji came to be known as Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji. People came to His Holiness for help with their worldly affairs, to be healed of physical afflictions, or for guidance in their spiritual practice.

Where the Datta Temple stands today, a large stage once occupied the place. It was called Saraswati Peetha, and sometimes Narayana Peetha. <1>After the Datta Temple was built, the Ashrama began to be called Avadhoota Datta Peetham.</1>

Popularly called Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Ashram, the Peetham is the headquarters of Sri Swamiji’s mission. It has grown over the years to an impressive stature and encompasses many aspects of the spiritual life: here one can study Yoga, the Vedas and Sanskrit, bhajans, music and much more.
Milestones from the Peetham’s own records, from the first installation to the newest shrines.
A straw hut in a field
Sri Swamiji moves to the present site on Ooty Road — then only a straw hut in a field, on barren land. The Ashram is established and Sri Sachchidanandeshwara is installed.

On 9 June 1978, during a week-long ceremony, Lord Datta is installed as Sri Kaalaagni Shamana Dattatreya. After the Datta Temple was built, the Ashrama began to be called Avadhoota Datta Peetham. The SGS Hospital opens for free medical services.
The Universal Prayer Hall is unveiled; in 1985 the SGS Veda Pathashala is founded to teach the Vedas in the traditional Gurukula system.
Sri Swamiji inaugurates Nada Mantapa, the Hall of Musical Tones, on 31 May 1998. Sri Datta Venkateshwara Kshetram follows in 1999 and the Pillar of Dharma in 2000.
On Rama Navami, 21 April 2002, the idol of Lord Datta is relocated to the centre of the Prayer Hall and re-consecrated.
The Kishkindha Moolika Bonsai Garden opens in 2005, followed in 2006 by the Vishwam Museum and Saptarshi Sarovara.
Shuka Vana and Karya Siddhi Hanuman
In Sri Swamiji’s 70th year, Shuka Vana, the rehabilitation centre for birds, is founded and the 70-foot Karya Siddhi Hanuman statue is consecrated.
On 14 December 2016 eight Bhairava idols are consecrated as per Shaiva Agama rites, where a tunnel once led towards Chamundi Hill when the Ashrama started in 1966.
On 28 December 2023 Sri Swamiji consecrates the temple of Mother Goddess Rajarajeshwari and unveils Hari Sannidhi, home to 2,108 rare Salagramas.

More than 80 branches across India — including 16 Ashrams for the 16 incarnations of Lord Dattatreya — and, in the Peetham’s directory, centres in eleven countries beyond India, among them the UK, USA, Malaysia, Trinidad, Canada and Australia.

Our mission, in our own words

Avadhoota Datta Peetham is an international spiritual, cultural and social welfare organization established by His Holiness Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji in 1966. Its many projects revolve upon the recognition of the intrinsic worth of every single human life.

At the heart of the Peetham

At the heart of the Peetham is Lord Dattatreya, the presiding deity who embodies the Sadguru, or Master Teacher, principle. Dattatreya the eternal teacher is the manifestation of the Triple Principle of <1>Sat</1> (Existence), <2>Chit</2> (Knowledge) and <3>Ananda</3> (Bliss).

He guides seekers on their journey from the shadows of the material world to the illumination of the inner soul. As Sri Swamiji propagates the teachings of Dattatreya Avadhoota, a Datta Temple has been built in the Ashram — the first of the several Datta temples established in India and abroad.
“Do all such deeds to others, which you expect from others.”
“Try to identify divinity in every being.”
Lord Dattatreya’s message of Universal Brotherhood

“Avadhoota Datta Peetham is a world renowned institution for the social, moral and spiritual welfare of mankind.” Sri Swamiji reminds people of their social responsibility towards their fellow beings.

“The Vedas are our priceless inheritance from the remote past and they need to be preserved and propagated.” The Pathashala teaches all four Vedas, and Veda examinations are held every year on a national scale.
Service to mankind is service to God
Sri Swamiji reminds us time and again that service to mankind is service to God — through hospitals and medical camps, schools, and Annadanam, by which all Ashram visitors are fed free.
Sri Swamiji welcomes everyone, including agnostics, atheists and people of any faith. The motto is to serve humanity without the barricades of caste, creed, race or religion.
Bhajan singing is one of the main methods Sri Swamiji propagates, so Divya Naama Sankeertana is a daily part of Ashram life — and music, practised with deep concentration, becomes a therapy.

“Bonsai trees and birds are my two eyes. Naada is my voice. My breath is the Veda.” — Sri Swamiji. Sri Swamiji promotes with zeal the preservation of flora and fauna: the Ashram houses Shuka Vana, the Bonsai garden, a Gau Shala and gardens of trees linked to the Rashis and Nakshatras.
The Ashram is situated on a sprawling 40-acre site at the foot of Chamundi Hill, in the Royal City of Mysuru. Its temples, auditorium, gardens, schools and hospital sit side by side.

Shelter for birds that were abused, injured or abandoned

Shuka Vana houses hundreds of colourful, exotic species of parrots, including many critically endangered and endangered species. His Holiness Sri Sri Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji has taken a serious resolve to rehabilitate injured birds, and Shuka Vana compassionately gives shelter to neglected and abandoned birds.

It provides a restored natural habitat in which endangered and critically endangered species can thrive and reproduce. The aviary’s healthy, safe and clean environment is instrumental in their protection and conservation, and the enclosure spans an entire acre within the Ashram grounds.

Visitors can watch rare parrot species flying freely. The Peetham describes the aviary as a place to be in the presence of the deity that presides over one’s own zodiac sign, and of a parrot that represents one’s planet and birth date.

Sri Swamiji believes that birds play a crucial role in the survival of other species. With bird populations declining in recent years, Shuka Vana aims to educate and sensitise the public, and to foster respect and kindness towards birds.
Most bird species in an aviary
Awarded at SGS Avadhoota Datta Peetham, Mysuru, for housing the most parrot species in a single aviary. The certificate records 468 species; the Peetham’s Shuka Vana pages give 486.

Shuka Vana was invited to take part in the “Year of the Bird 2018” project, led by Audubon, BirdLife International, the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and National Geographic with 190 other organisations, to protect birds and their habitats.
How the birds are cared for
The units that care for the <1>birds</1>

The parrots are arranged according to their nativity and behaviour inside a well-protected, two-layered meshed aviary, planted with selected plants and trees, with food stations, water pots and nest boxes.
Shelter for injured and handicapped birds and birds with mental illness, including physically challenged birds that were not receiving proper care with their owners.
Diagnostics and treatment for the birds, supported by laboratories and a radiology unit.
PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) for gender determination and to detect viral and bacterial diseases, with an airfuge, water bath, vortex mixer, electrophoresis unit and gel documentation unit.
X-ray machine, ultrasound scan machine, inhalant anaesthesia machine and oxygen concentrator.
Bio-safety cabinet, incubator, autoclave and binocular microscope.
When a bird is diagnosed with an illness or disease, it is isolated and shifted here, where it is given treatment.
Fruits and vegetables are cleaned and cut and grains are sprouted, then weighed and dispatched for the birds.
A nutritious, hygienic and balanced diet, along with a special hand-feeding formula. Food and water quality checks are done routinely in the lab.
Parrots do not show symptoms of illness, so each bird is individually examined once every 45 days. The medicines used are avian-specific.
Protecting parrots that are endangered in the wild
Conservation of various species, especially endangered and critically endangered birds, is undertaken at Shuka Vana.

Wonders of Mother Nature, in miniature

The trees are displayed in the tranquil surroundings of Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Ashram. A keen nature lover, Sri Swamiji has a special interest in developing spiritual gardens that enlighten people about the divinity of Mother Nature, and the Ashram owes its lush look to his enduring attention to detail and the dedicated volunteer garden staff.
The towering sculpture of <1>Moolikeswara</1>, the presiding deity of herbal healing, who frees addicts from their addictions, adorns the garden.

Every tree in the Bonsai Garden has a history behind it. Sri Swamiji goes to each tree and listens to its raga, or the sounds it makes, and has brought many trees from different countries; from Calcutta came a bonsai Neem tree.
These gardens stand testimony to Sri Swamiji’s zeal for evolving new ways of adoring and worshipping nature.

Kishkindha Moolika Vana, then called Madhuvana, was safeguarded by Dadhimukha, uncle of the monkey king Sugreeva. When news came that Sita had been found, the jubilant Vanaras destroyed his garden of short fruit trees, snuggled between two hills. The Peetham holds that India has had the bonsai tradition since the Treta Yuga.
The leaf that saved a child

As a child, Sri Swamiji swallowed nine pellets of rat poison smeared with honey. His father Narasimha Sastry, a physician, sent for a leaf from a forest tree, and its juice saved the boy’s life. Years later his father told him of kubja (midget) trees grown in small pots for medicine; at about thirty, Sri Swamiji’s interest in bonsai was rekindled.

The year Sri Swamiji was born, his mother planted a tree in the precincts of the Sangameswara Siva temple at Mekedatu. Entwined by snakes, the Naga devatas, it grew twisted. Devotees found it during the temple’s renovation and brought it to the Bonsai Garden, where it can be seen today.

Sri Swamiji organises Bonsai Conventions that bring together enthusiasts, professional tree experts and hobbyists from different countries to share their expertise, their love for the art and their commitment to preserving nature. Techniques for different aesthetic styles, and methods for preserving tree species, are explained and explored.

He urges every child and adult to adopt not one tree but several, and, where space is limited, to learn bonsai techniques to safeguard tree species at least in miniature form. Sri Swamiji has also written a book on growing bonsai at home.

Nada Mantapa is equipped with state-of-the-art sound, lighting and theatrical systems. It stands as a testament to Sri Swamiji’s dedication to the healing and meditative powers of music: a venue for world-class performances, and a sanctuary where the transformative power of music can be experienced in its purest form.

Sri Swamiji frequently performs “Music for Meditation and Healing” here. During the 10th anniversary celebrations of Nada Mantapa on 29 May 2008, his handling of Raga Veenavadini captivated the audience.
Large portraits of renowned composers adorn the walls. When Saint Tyagaraja’s “Samaja Varagamana” is played or sung, the lights in front of Tyagaraja’s portrait illuminate automatically.

Picturesque Mekedatu is near Brahma Kundam, where Sri Swamiji was born, amidst the Sahyadri hills at the confluence of three rivers, near the Sangameswara temple. A Siva Lingam found at the spot where Sri Swamiji’s home stood gave the Ashram the name Datta Kashi.

To protect Manginapudi (Tallapalem) from severe cyclones and strong tidal waves, Sri Swamiji consecrated Lord Dattatreya at the seaside temple of Lord Nagareswara in 1991, and had twelve wells dug, each with healing waters of different constituents. Popularly called Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Ashram, the Peetham is situated on a sprawling 40-acre site at the foot of Chamundi Hill, in the royal city of Mysuru. This is the headquarters of Sri Swamiji’s mission.

Here one can study Yoga, the Vedas and Sanskrit, bhajans and music, and in the Universal Prayer Hall traditional Pujas and Homas are performed. The first of the sixteen Datta Kshetras stands here, the temple the Peetham calls the primordial and central seat of Datta Peetham’s global reach.

<1>Lord Datta descends.</1> In a week-long ceremony from 4 to 11 June, Lord Datta was installed as Sri Kaalaagni Shamana Dattatreya on 9 June. A stage called Saraswati Peetha, sometimes Narayana Peetha, once stood here; after the Datta Temple was built, the Ashrama began to be called Avadhoota Datta Peetham. That week Sri Swamiji introduced Datta worship, the Datta Stava and the greeting <2>Jaya Guru Deva Datta</2>, which became <3>Jaya Guru Datta</3> in the mid-eighties.
<1>The Universal Prayer Hall</1> is unveiled. Every evening devotees gather here for Divya Naama Sankeertana and the Kakada Arati, lighting sixteen lamps before Lord Datta.
<1>Re-consecration.</1> On Rama Navami, 21 April 2002, the idol of Lord Datta was relocated to the centre of the Prayer Hall and re-consecrated.

What are the temple darshan timings?
The Peetham’s homepage gives the Temple Timings as 6 AM – 12 PM in the morning and 4 PM – 8 PM in the evening, and lists Abhisheka at 7 AM and Aarti at 6 PM daily at the Hanuman temple.
Some shrines keep their own hours: the Karya Siddhi Hanuman and Sri Datta Venkateshwara temple pages list different weekday and weekend timings. Please check the temple you plan to visit.
Can I stay at the Ashram?

Persons of all faiths are welcome, but facilities are limited and are primarily maintained for devotees of Sri Swamiji. Visitors are requested to stay in hotels in Mysuru and visit the Ashram daily for its programmes.

Those seeking a brief stay should first attend Ashram programmes consistently for at least a week; the Ashram Administrator handles such inquiries. No visitors may stay while Sri Swamiji or Sri Bala Swamiji are out of station, and during major functions all newcomers must find accommodation elsewhere.
Whom do I ask for permission to visit and stay?

Even those known to the Ashram staff and to Sri Swamiji should ask in advance, by letter, phone, fax or email, to H. V. Prasad, personal secretary to Sri Swamiji. Once your plans are final, notify the Ashram of your arrival date, the number in your party and your expected duration of stay.

Carry photocopies of a Government-approved identity proof or passport, and passport photos, for every member of your family or group; they are submitted to the Ashrama office on arrival, as a government regulation.
How do I reach the Ashram?

The Ashram is at Datta Nagar on Ooty Road (Nanjangud Road), Mysuru. For a first visit from overseas the Peetham recommends flying to Bengaluru and hiring a taxi to Mysuru from the desks in the airport arrival hall.
In Mysuru, city bus 119 runs from the City Bus Stand directly to the Ashram, and 119A goes via JSS Medical College. Auto rickshaws and cabs from the railway station take about 15–20 minutes.

What if I arrive late at night?
The Ashram’s gates close at 11 PM, so if you arrive late at night, please stay in a hotel. Travelling by road from Bengaluru to Mysuru after 9 PM is not advised.

As its name implies, the Universal Prayer Hall is an auditorium where daily congregational prayers take place, drawing a large number of devotees who gather in the divine presence of Sri Swamiji. It houses the main deity of the Peetham — <1>Kaalaagni Shamana Dattatreya Swami</1>.

The most revered worship, the Sri Chakra Puja, is performed at the Sri Chakram Meru, enshrined in a special Mantap to the right side. To truly appreciate the sanctity of this Puja, one must witness it in person.
On the right of the hall, the Panchayatana Devasthana houses five small temples; on the left, a Shivalaya is dedicated to Lord Shiva as Sachchidanandeshwara.

As devotees circumambulate the deity they see the intricately designed forms of the Nava Durgas, the miniature forms of the deities of the 18 Shakti Peethams, and several Devi Yantras and Mandalams. Sri Swamiji has also installed a big <1>Sri Chakra</1>, to which devotees can personally offer prayers with Kumkum Archana.

The most spectacular Hari Sannidhi stands to the immediate right of the Rajarajeshwari temple, unveiled by Sri Swamiji on 28 December 2023.

The Trivikrama Salagrama and the Manoratha Kurma Salagrama, weighing 300 kg, have also been installed inside the Sannidhi. A specially made <1>Sudarshana Yantra</1> on top of the Sannidhi was designed and conceptualised by Sri Swamiji.

For those seeking spirituality and peace, a visit to Sri Datta Venkateswara Kshetram is a must. Pilgrims say that this temple for Lord Venkateswara pulsates with Divine Energy. Its architecture is much like the one in holy Tirumala, and it is the firm belief of Datta devotees that the Lord of the seven hills has Himself come to Datta Peetham.

Before the temple stands a huge <1>Dhwaja Stambha</1> — the sacred flag post — made from a 150-year-old teak tree, brought from the deep forests of Kerala. Several thousands throng the temple on Vaikuntha Ekadashi every year, and Annadanam is conducted for the needy on every Purnima.

The Ashta Bhairava temple was consecrated by His Holiness Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji on 14 December 2016. Eight Bhairava idols were consecrated as per Shaiva Agama rites, in the south-east corner of the Ashrama.

The continuous succession of Gurus — from Adi Guru Dattatreya, through Sripada Vallabha and Narasimha Saraswati, to Sri Swamiji, our present Guru.

“Guru Parampara” is the combination of two words, Guru and Parampara. As per the sacred text Guru Geeta, the dialog between Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, the word “Guru” comprises of two words, “Gu” and “Ru”.
<1>“Parampara”</1> means “uninterrupted succession”. So, <2>Guru Parampara is the continuous succession or lineage of Gurus.</2>
No one can be at par with the Guru

All scriptures declare emphatically that Guru is the very embodiment of divine and spiritual knowledge (Gnaana). Every seeker needs the guidance of a Guru to progress on the path of the spiritual ladder.

It is not only a customary practice to offer prayers to the lineage of Gurus but also a fundamental duty of a seeker, for no one can be at par with the Guru or is as supreme as Him. Prayer and Pooja to the Guru is performed to offer gratitude to the lineage of Gurus who have bestowed divine wisdom. By doing so, one is blessed with knowledge of the Supreme.

To get rid of the afflictions of one’s mind and to ascend the spiritual ladder, it is a must to seek a Guru in a physical form, serve him with reverence and devotion, and thereby cleanse oneself of sins and impurities.
One must pray to Guru, before and after completion of any work. Without Guru, one cannot reach one’s goal.
<1>Gu</1><2>In this context, “Gu” implies He is above all attributes (<3>gunas</3>).</2>
As He is the absolute Supreme Lord who is beyond traits and form, He has been addressed as Guru.
<1>Lord Dattatreya</1>Adi Guru — the Guru of Gurus

According to the determination of Brahma and as a consequence of the great penance of Sage Atri and Anasuya in the Kriya Yuga (the Krita Yuga of the Peetham’s glossary, the first of the Yugas / eons), Dattatreya, combining all the aspects of the Trinity — Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva — incarnated for the sake of his devotees.

The word “Datta” means the one who has given himself, and since he was born to Sage Atri, he came to be known as Lord Dattatreya. Dattatreya Swami is known as the Guru of Gurus since he was the foremost Guru who promoted and propagated the divine knowledge. Hence He is extolled as “Adi Guru”.

Datta’s incarnation has a unique feature: while other incarnations return to their original abode as soon as their respective tasks are completed, Dattatreya’s incarnation remains permanently on Earth as Guru Murti, exerting an eternal influence.
<1>Jaya Guru Datta</1> — the motto of Avadhoota Datta Peetham, and the greeting devotees share with each other.

Lord Datta has three heads and six hands, with four dogs around Him and Kaamadhenu (cow) and a Kalpavruksha (Audumbara tree) behind Him. The four dogs represent the four Vedas — Rig, Yajur, Saama and Atharvana — while the Kaamadhenu and Kalpavruksha represent wish fulfilment of the devotees.
One hand wields the Shula (trident), which is meant for killing the ego. One more hand holds the Damaruga (drum) to awaken the people who are always in the state of slumber called ajnana (ignorance).
The Shankha (conch) represents the primordial sound Omkara — when it is blown, avidya (ignorance) vanishes. The Chakra is symbolic of karma, like a round circle with neither a beginning nor an end.
The rosary’s many rounded beads represent the universes in multitude under the Lord’s control. The Kamandalu (water-pot) does not contain ordinary water; it has the nectar of wisdom.

One prominent story associated with Lord Dattatreya is his preaching to his disciple King Yadu about his twenty-four Gurus of nature, from whom he learned profound lessons about spirituality and life.
Patience and doing good to others in one’s entire life can be learnt from Mother Earth.
Air is symbolic of the qualities of non attachment and stainlessness.
Sky represents the all pervading nature and about the Self that remains uncontaminated by the qualities that arise in the elements forming the body.
Water represents purity, smoothness and sweetness, so one should have a pure heart, speak sweet words and be full of love for all beings.

Even though fire consumes all things indiscriminately, it does not become unholy, so too, one should have knowledge, should be a tapasvin, be undesirable and remain unaffected by what others offer him.
Waxing and waning are only for Moon’s lustre, likewise, the delinquencies of the six senses are of the body only and not of the Atman.
Sun absorbs water from Earth with its rays and returns the water to Earth at an appropriate time. Similarly, one should accept the objects of the senses without any enthusiasm for them.
A pigeon develops too much attachment or friendship and ends up in affliction. So, attachments lead to one’s downfall and waste of precious lifespan.
Like a python, one should forego even sleep and food, and remain firmly devoted to the Self.

An ocean does not let even a small leaf to land on its surface, so too one should not allow even the smallest desire or agitation to enter into the mind. Moreover, many rivers flow into an ocean, yet it does not overflow. Likewise, one should not be over joyous when desires are fulfilled or be depressed when they do not materialize.

Deluded by the flames of fire and expecting to enjoy comforts, the moth rushes towards the flames and gets burnt. So, man must be careful not to fall a victim to the attractions of a woman or to the delusion caused by the sense organs.
A bee gathers nectar from almost every flower, so too one should study all scriptures, skilfully grasp the essence and adapt it in the search for the Self.
Although elephant is very strong and intelligent, it gets trapped due to its lustfulness. So too, one should know that lust is dangerous.

The honey-thief contrives and steals the honey that is hoarded by honey bees. Therefore, if a person is stingy and hides his wealth without enjoying it himself or allowing others to share it, he risks being robbed by someone.

The hunter’s music makes the innocent deer to stand still and listen with closed eyes. Sage Rushyashrunga became a victim of a dancing girl attracted to her music and dance. So too, one should not be beguiled by music or dancing.
The uncontrolled tongue of a fish makes it the prey of the fisherman’s hook. Therefore, a fish teaches that controlling and conquering the tongue is very important.

Pingala, a harlot, attained marvellous tranquility, peace of mind and a sound sleep by giving up the desire for wealth and lustful pleasures. So, desire is sorrow and absence of wants is the highest happiness.

A little bird holding a bit of meat gets attacked by a bigger and stronger bird. When the bird drops the meat, the other bird follows to get the meat piece. So too, if one keeps a thing coveted by others, one will be subjected to severe anguish and therefore it is wise to give up such things voluntarily.
A little child is worry-free and is always happy playing by himself. One should also remain happy like a child.
When a maiden pounds the paddy, her bangles make jingling sound. To avoid any sound, she retains only one bangle on each wrist. Likewise, quarrels ensue when too many persons gather in one place.
An arrow-maker has utmost concentration in making arrows. Likewise, one should sit with total focus and practice Yoga.
A serpent is always vigilant and is never absent-minded. Unlike a man, a snake does not waste its time building a shelter and happily lives in an ant-hill deserted by ants.
A spider stirs the threads in its stomach and with that material weaves its web, plays with it and finally swallows it. The process of creation also is akin to a spider’s web.

Like how the form of an insect that stares hard at a dragon-fly undergoes a change, so too, one attains the form of those on whom one concentrates the mind completely. If a small insect can transform its body, even a man possessing intellect and the faculty of meditation and concentration can be certainly liberated.
Lord Dattatreya’s teachings promote detachment from material desires and ego. He has preached the essence of Universal Brotherhood in these simple sentences:
“Observe any object or creature, try to emulate the good in them or shun the evil aspects evident; you can always add value to your life.”

A science of meditation and a skilful way of living: the Kriya Yoga of Adi Guru Dattatreya, taught by Sri Swamiji to seekers in the East and the West since 1966.
<1>Sri Swamiji teaches Datta Kriya Yoga</1>In the lineage of Adi Guru Dattatreya

Derived from the Sanskrit <1>yuj</1>, yoga signifies union: the individual soul (<2>jeevatma</2>) merging with the Universal Soul (<3>Paramatma</3>), Sachchidananda Swaroopa. <4>Kriya</4> denotes action. Kriya Yoga channels the life-force energy (<5>praana</5>) through mental processes to achieve this union, starting with <6>pranayama</6>, the control of breath.

According to the Markandeya Purana, the eternal Guru Dattatreya taught this mystic Kriya Yoga to Subramanya Swamy. Because it was bestowed by Lord Dattatreya, it is known as Datta Kriya Yoga. Vaamadeva, Jadabharata, Sukadeva, Parasurama, Prahlada, Alarka and Kartaviryarjuna all became great Yogis through it.
Sri Swamiji teaches Datta Kriya Yoga in the lineage of Adi Guru Dattatreya, drawing inspiration from his mother and Guru, Sri Jayalakshmi Mata, a Master of Raja Yoga and Sree Vidya.
“The intelligent man, having known the Effulgent One by means of Adhyatma Yoga (meditation on the inner self), abandons both joy and sorrow.”
“The Rishis (seers) absorbed in Dhyana Yoga (the yoga of meditation) realized the Soul Power of the Supreme concealed by the gunas (qualities).”
Dhyaanaavasthita tadgatena manasaa pashyanti yam yoginah
“Whom the Yogis behold with their minds engrossed in THAT, through meditation.”
Every chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is termed “yoga”, and the entire Gita is designated as Yoga Shastra.
Focused yogic breathing quietens the mind and directs the flow of vital energy (prana) through the entire body. Prana is the vital life force that sustains and awakens our subtle energy system.

Ancient yogis viewed lifespan in terms of breaths, with rapid breathing linked to shorter lifespans. Datta Kriya Yoga offers accessible practices to improve health by regulating breath, regardless of physical condition or lifestyle.
The circle is illustrative, a quiet aid to breath awareness. It is not a timed exercise; learn the techniques from a Datta Kriya Yoga teacher.
Sri Swamiji has renewed the Kriya Yoga principle: the encapsulation of Hatha Yoga, the exercise-based yoga practice of today, and Raja Yoga, which involves mind control through breath control.

<1>Meaning.</1> I salute those sacred Sadguru padukas on which are depicted symbolically Lord Vishnu along with Sree Devi (Goddess of Wealth) and Bhoodevi (Goddess of Earth), Agastya (Saint) and other lines, and also several seed letters of occult nature.

mūlādhāraṁ tathā svādhiṣṭhānaṁ ca manipūrakam<1/>anāhatam viśuddhākhyam ājñācakram vidurbudhāh<2/>tavādhāra svarūpāṇī konacakrani pārvāti<3/>trikona rupini śaktih bindurūpaḥ(s) śivassmrtah<4/>avinābhāva sambandhah tasmāt bindu trikonayoh ||

<1>Meaning.</1> The learned Seers say that the transcendental spiritual energy called ‘Kundalini’ resides in Moolaadhaara and pervades the Swadhishtana, Manipooraka, Anahata, Vishuddha and Ajna Chakras (pranic energy distribution centres in the body). The Goddess Parvati, based in these chakras in the form of triangles, energises the chakras. The energy in the form of a triangle has at its centre the Bindu (dot), the form of Siva. Therefore an inseparable relationship exists between Shiva and Shakti.

mūlādhāre ganapati vapurdhārinam deśikendram |<1/>svādhishthāne dhratavidhitanum sādhakoddāra dakṣam |<2/>jvālāvarṇam rucira manipūrāntare rudramūrtim |<3/>nādātmānam vitata mahitānāhatākāśa purnām |<4/>bhāmārdhāngam paramapuruṣākāra gamyam viśuddhe |<5/>jyotīrūpam vikti rahitam tattvamajñātārāle |<6/>svātmārāmam dvayavirahitam tam sahasrāra padme |<7/>dhyāyāmi tvām ganapati gurum saccidānanda rūpam |

<1>Meaning.</1> To that Supreme Master who resides in the Moolaadhaara Chakra in the form of Lord Ganapathy; who resides in the Swadhishtana Chakra in the form of Lord Brahma, elevating the sadhaka (spiritual practitioner); who abides in the Manipooraka Chakra radiating the redness of fire in the form of Lord Rudra (Shiva); who dwells in the Anahata Chakra and fills all space (akash) with sound; who is resplendent like Lord Ardhanarishwara (Shiva) as the ultimate Purusha (Supreme Soul) in the Vishuddha Chakra; who, located in the Ajna Chakra, illumines without change as the principles of light and wisdom; who, beyond duality, as one without a second, exists in the absolute state of Atman (Self) and Universal Consciousness in the thousand-petal lotus — to Him, the Ganapati Guru, the embodiment of sat-chit-ananda (truth-knowledge-bliss), I offer my prayers again and again.

Raga Ragini Vidya · Music for Meditation & Healing

Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji is widely recognised for His transformative Divya Naama Sankeertana — singing the divine names — and for Healing & Meditation Music that has touched countless lives around the world.
<1>Raga Saama</1>, as presented on screen during a Music for Meditation & Healing concert: the raga with its zodiac sign, element and chakra.

Rooted in ancient Vedic teaching as <1>nāda cikitsā</1>, healing through sound is what the world now calls music therapy. Several decades of deep, intuitive research into the effects of musical notes and rhythms on the human body have given Sri Swamiji a profound knowledge of effective music therapy.

Coupling this with the ancient Indian science of Raga Ragini Vidya, He plays Healing Music for audiences across the world. In concert He alternates between melodies that relax and melodies that energise, accompanied by musicians on classical Indian instruments.
“Only a Nadayogi adept in the aspects of traditional as well as the modern sciences is able to blend the art of music with healing music therapeutic medicine and perform Nada Chikitsa.”

The subtle body comprises 72,000 Naadis; 14 are considered most significant for carrying praana from the subtle to the physical body. A disruption in the Naadis can lead to physical or mental ailments.
The flow of sound vibration — naada — parallels the flow of praana. Specific raagas are associated with healing specific organs of the body, aligned with the flow of praana through the Naadis.
Thoughts manifest as sound in the mind. Healing music introduces higher vibrations that calm, and eventually control, the daily influx of thoughts, preparing the mind for meditation.

When Nada, the pure sound of melody, is approached reverentially and absorbed with total concentration, its vibrations “clear the dust off the mirror-like mind”, and the inherent divinity in man is reflected.
Lowered blood pressure, a stabilised heart rate, improved motor skills and relief from pain.
Reduced depression and anxiety, strengthened memory and enhanced intellectual activity.

Because His compositions are so prolific, the title <1>Sagara</1> — ocean — was given to express this form of Raga-Ragini.

Inaugurated by Sri Swamiji on 31 May 1998, this purpose-built auditorium at the Mysuru Ashram has hosted thousands of concerts. It is equipped with state-of-the-art sound, lighting and theatrical systems.
<1>Illustrative diagram, not to scale.</1> Seats fan out radially within 140° of the performer, in the shape of a palm-leaf hand fan.

The fan-shaped design was inspired by an episode Sri Swamiji narrates: Lord Rama, seeking Seetha in the forest, was fanned by Hanuman with a palm leaf. The auditorium takes the shape of that palm-leaf fan, with its entrance facing east towards the sacred Chamundi hills.

Large portraits of the great composers line the walls. When a composer’s work is performed, the lights before that portrait illuminate — when Saint Tyagaraja’s “Samaja Varagamana” is sung, Tyagaraja’s portrait glows.
Twenty-two colossal sculpted Tamburas stand against its pillars, representing the 22 Shrutis (microtones) of the Sangeeta Shastra.

Pillars of Service · Avadhoota Datta Peetham
From the Goshala and the Veda Pathashala to SGS Hospital, daily Annadana and the birds of Shuka Vana, the Peetham serves humanity without the barricades of caste, creed, race or religion.
Avadhoota Datta Peetham provides medical, educational, vocational and spiritual services to the needy. Compassion here reaches cows, children, patients and birds alike.

<1>Sri Swamiji</1>Sri Swamiji emphasises that spiritual life includes service to those in need. This practice, called Karma Yoga, means working selflessly and surrendering the fruits of one’s actions to God.

Kamadhenu, Kalpavriksha, Amruta and Mother Lakshmi emerged together in creation as the most splendorous embodiments of divinity. The scriptures declare that all Devatas reside in the cow, so Sanatana Dharma reveres her as <1>Gomaata</1>.
Sri Swamiji has established a large Goshala at the Mysuru Ashram that shelters and cares for more than 50 cows, with Goshalas maintained at other branches too.

Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Veda Pathashala, founded in 1985, teaches all four Vedas and Sanskrit in the traditional Gurukula system — nurturing young students in the living Vedic tradition while preparing them for the modern world.

Around 120 students are pursuing Vedic education at the Mysuru Ashram, and the Peetham also runs Veda Pathashalas in Pithapuram and Jayalakshmipuram (Bommeparti), Andhra Pradesh. Sri Swamiji calls Sanskrit not a language but a “Bhava”, a feeling. The Junior Pontiff, Sri Bala Swamiji, is Himself an alumnus.

Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Hospital operates a comprehensive healthcare system within the Holistic Health Centre, providing preventive and curative care: outpatient services in Ayurveda, Allopathy, Homeopathy, Naturopathy and other systems, and Ayurvedic inpatient care.
Sri Swamiji always emphasises primary health care, rather than spending lakhs of rupees on tertiary health care.

Every month, SGS Hospital attends to 5,000–10,000 people. A Mobile Dispensary Van regularly visits the villages around Mysuru, and the hospital takes part in national programmes such as Immunization and Pulse-Polio. The Holistic Health Centre was inaugurated by former President of India Sri R. Venkataraman and then Chief Minister of Karnataka Sri S.M. Krishna.

Sri Swamiji was born at the sacred confluence of three rivers — Arkavati, Kaveri and Guptagaamini — at Mekedatu, Karnataka, to the pious Brahmin couple Narasimha Shastry, later known as Sri Narahari Teertha Swami, and Jayalakshmi Maata, on 26 May 1942.

His actual birth occurred on a rock in the Kaveri river. His mother was in deep meditation, and the child was born covered with holy ash. He was named <1>Satyanarayana</1>. A Muslim saint had predicted to His parents that their child would have supreme wisdom and knowledge, and was destined to uplift mankind.
<1>Sri Jayalakshmi Maata Aradhana</1>Sri Swamiji worships His mother every single day.

Sri Swamiji’s mother, Sri Jayalakshmi Maata, was His first Guru and initiated Him into spiritual life. She bestowed Sri Vidya and Raja Yoga, and explained the esoteric meanings of the Vedas, Puranas, Mahabharata and Ramayana.
At the tender age of eleven, in the Anjaneya Temple at Bommeparti, she transmitted spiritual energy — <1>Shaktipaatam</1> — to the child. She attained Maha Samadhi the same year, 1953.

Satyanarayana completed His schooling like other children, but found that school had nothing to offer Him. He sang bhajans and kirtans for His friends, and gave Yoga classes in small village huts or on river banks while wandering the countryside as a monk.
<1>The Universal Prayer Hall</1>“The crown of the Ashram,” in Sri Swamiji’s words.

In 1966 Sri Swamiji moved to the present site of the Mysuru Ashram on Ooty Road — in those early days only a straw hut in a field. The land was barren and infested with cobras and scorpions. He slept under the trees on the bare ground with these creatures crawling all around Him, and was never harmed.

It was there, at Mysuru, that He came to be known as <1>Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji</1>. The same year He was initiated into Sanyasa at Srisailam and installed Sri Sachchidanandeshwara at the Mysuru Ashram.
People come to Him for help with their worldly affairs, to be healed of physical afflictions, or for guidance in their spiritual practice.

The grand welcome arch with Hanuman idols.
Visitors enter through the grand Hanumadwaram, a magnificently sculpted welcome arch with Hanuman idols. Just beyond it, an intricate carving of the infant form of Lord Dattatreya greets them.
366 pillars, one for each birth date.
366 pillars stand on either side of a pathway in the Ashrama. Called the “Date of Birth Pillars”, each carries the deity and demigod for that particular day.

Daily congregational prayers are held here in the divine presence of Sri Swamiji. The hall houses the main deity of the Peetham, Kaalaagni Shamana Dattatreya, with the Sri Chakram Meru beside Him, and the Panchayatana Devasthana and the Sachchidanandeshwara Shivalaya on either side.
The Nava Durgas and the deities of the 18 Shakti Peethams.

Consecrated by Sri Swamiji on 28 December 2023, beside the Universal Prayer Hall. Around the Goddess are the Nava Durgas, miniature forms of the deities of the 18 Shakti Peethams, and a big Sri Chakra where devotees offer Kumkum Archana.

To the immediate right of the Rajarajeshwari temple, it houses 2,108 rare Salagramas in the form of Ananthanaga Shayana, with the Trivikrama and Manoratha Kurma Salagramas weighing 300 kg. A Sudarshana Yantra conceived by Sri Swamiji crowns the Sannidhi.

Devotees offer Pooja here to Sri Datta Venkateshwara Swamy, Goddess Padmavati, Dhanvantari, Sarva Doshahara Shiva, Sri Marakata Subrahmanya Swamy, Lord Karyasiddhi Hanuman and the Navagraha Devatas. Thousands come for Vaikuntha Ekadashi every year.
As listed on the <1>Sri Datta Venkateshwara Temple page</1>.
Consecrated by Sri Swamiji in 2012, the 70-ft monolithic statue is the tallest stone statue of Hanuman in India. On weekends, 3D projection mapping is synchronised with the Hanuman Chalisa.
Eight Bhairavas in a subterranean shrine.

Eight Bhairava idols, consecrated as per Shaiva Agama rites in the south-east corner of the Ashrama. The subterranean temple has a main shrine for the Pradhana Bhairava, with the other seven in niches around it.

A purpose-built music auditorium shaped like a palm-leaf fan, its entrance facing east toward the Chamundi hills. It holds 22 sculpted Tamburas for the 22 Shrutis, 72 pillars for the 72 Melakarta ragas and the world’s first Sapta Swara Devata Mantapam.

Founded by Sri Swamiji in 2012, with its own bird hospital. The free-flight walk-in aviary is home to more than 2,000 birds of 486 species. Its Guinness World Record (6 May 2017) is for the most bird species in an aviary; the certificate records 468.
Closed on Wednesdays. Timings vary across official sources, and the Shuka Vana page says it is temporarily closed for maintenance; please check with the Ashram before visiting.

More than 450 carefully shaped miniature trees in an oriental garden setting, nurtured by Sri Swamiji Himself. Moolikeswara, presiding deity of herbal healing, stands here among the Navagraha, Sapta Rishi, Nakshatra and Rashi gardens.
Closed on Wednesdays. Hours from the Bonsai Garden page. Timings vary across official sources; please check with the Ashram before visiting.

“Vishwam” means “Universe”. The museum displays rare gifts Sri Swamiji received from devotees worldwide, from crystals and minerals to antiques, with His stamp collection (specimens from as far back as 1835) and musical instruments from over forty countries.
Inaugurated in 2006, with the Vishwam Museum.
A sarovara (pond) in the Ashram grounds, inaugurated in 2006, the same year as the Vishwam Museum.
Free consultation and medicines at the polyclinic.

Outpatient services in Ayurveda, Allopathy, Homeopathy, Naturopathy and other systems of medicine, with free consultation, counselling and medicines at the Allopathy polyclinic. It attends to 5,000–10,000 people every month.
All four Vedas and Sanskrit, in the Gurukula way.
Classes in all four Vedas and in Sanskrit, in the traditional Gurukula system. Around 120 students are pursuing Vedic education here.
Care for more than 50 cows, and Gau Pooja.
Sri Swamiji has established a large Goshala at the Mysuru Ashram that shelters and cares for more than 50 cows. Devotees may offer Gau Pooja, worship of Gau Mata, here.

Persons of all faiths are welcome at Avadhoota Datta Peetham. However, facilities are limited and are primarily maintained to accommodate devotees of His Holiness Sri Sri Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Swamiji.
Visitors are therefore requested to obtain hotel accommodation in the city of Mysuru and visit the Ashram daily to attend its programmes and activities. <1>See hotels near the Ashram</1>.

Those seeking a brief stay on the Ashram premises should attend Ashram programmes consistently for at least a week or more before inquiring about staying. The Ashram Administrator handles such inquiries.
No visitors are permitted to stay while Sri Swamiji or Sri Balaswamiji are out of station.
During major functions, all newcomers are required to find accommodation elsewhere.

Even those known to the Ashram staff and to Sri Swamiji should ask permission in advance before making arrangements to visit and stay in the Ashram. Permission may be sought by letter, phone, fax or email to <1>H. V. Prasad, personal secretary to Sri Swamiji</1>, well ahead of your travel plans.
Once your plans are finalised, notify the Ashram of your arrival date, the number in your party and your expected duration of stay. <1>Contact details</1>.

Please carry photocopies of a Government-approved identity proof or passport, and passport photos, for every member of your family or group. Submit them to the Ashrama office on arrival: it is a government regulation.
First-time overseas travellers may find this helpful. It is best to begin travel preparations weeks or even months before your journey.
Procure a current, valid passport from the government of your country.
Apply to the Indian Consulate (Embassy) in your country for a visa that allows you to enter and stay in India for a designated period. Indian Consulates are usually located in major cities.
A three- or six-month tourist visa may suffice. Those wishing to stay longer should apply for a different type of visa.
Please do not list Datta Peetham as the responsible party for your visit to India.

Your travel agent can provide the information you need for the journey, such as how to apply for a passport, the addresses and phone numbers of Indian Consulates, baggage allowances and weight limits. Their primary job is to provide your flight tickets; prices can vary dramatically depending on the airline you choose.

Wherever you depart from, fly to Bengaluru, in Karnataka, for your first visit. Your travel agent may arrange a connecting flight from Mumbai, Delhi or Chennai. Several airlines now fly directly to Bengaluru, including Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, Malaysian Airlines, British Airways, Emirates and Gulf Air; arriving directly removes the hassle of staying in Mumbai or Delhi at night.
Allow ample time for connecting flights so that you can clear customs and change airlines. You may need to change from an international to a domestic airport, depending on your first city of entry.
In the arrival hall at Bengaluru airport there are several taxi stand desks where you can hire a taxi directly to Mysuru.

At Sri Ganapathy Sachchidananda Ashram, devotee etiquette is an integral part of the spiritual journey and community life: a holistic approach to spiritual living, emphasising reverence, devotion, service and community.
Respect Ashramites, local people and all visitors

Show respect and reverence towards the Gurus, Sri Swamiji and Sri Balaswamiji, the Peethadhipati and the Uttaradhikaari of Avadhoota Datta Peetham, following their guidance and teachings with humility and sincerity.

Maintain reverence and decorum on entering the Ashram premises and sacred areas such as temples and meditation halls: observe silence, remove footwear and refrain from any behaviour that may disturb the peaceful atmosphere.
Take part in the daily rituals and activities, such as Sri Chakra Puja, Homa and Divya Naama Sankeertana (bhajan) sessions. Devotees may also sponsor these rituals as a form of devotion.
During Maha Shivaratri, Sri Swamiji’s Birthday celebrations, Navaratri and Datta Jayanti, join the processions, poojas, cultural performances and devotional singing with reverence and enthusiasm.
Adhere to the rules set by the Ashram administration, including codes of conduct, dress and behavioural norms that uphold the sanctity of the Ashram.

Devotees may offer selfless service within the Ashram community: temple maintenance, cooking, cleaning, or helping with social welfare programmes. Service is a form of devotion and an opportunity for spiritual growth.
Cultivate humility, compassion, patience and gratitude in daily life, reflecting the teachings and values of the Ashram’s spiritual tradition.
Respect all beings and treat everyone with kindness and compassion, regardless of differences in background, culture or beliefs.
The focus of interest for anyone should be the darshan and presence of Sri Swamiji and His teachings.
